title: Exxon, the world's largest oil company, enters the 1980s
what: Exxon, the former Standard Oil of New Jersey, is the largest oil company in the world and America's largest industrial company by sales. It finds, refines and sells oil on every continent and sells petrol as Exxon and Esso. Flush with cash from dearer oil, it has spread into new fields: in 1979 it paid 1.236 billion dollars for Reliance Electric, a maker of electric motors, and it is building an office-equipment business, Exxon Office Systems.
why: The listing beat: the safest big name of the oil boom, at a moment when oil money was being spent on diversification that Exxon would unwind within seven years. A player who buys here owns the benchmark oil stock for the whole game.
source: https://www.upi.com/Archives/1986/12/11/Exxon-Corp-in-a-surprise-move-Thursday-announced-it/2986534661200/ (Reliance price paid in 1979) (read 2026-10-03); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_ExxonMobil (name, diversification, Exxon Office Systems) (read 2026-10-03); https://www.upi.com/Archives/1981/04/16/Exxon-again-largest-firm-on-Fortune-500-list/3374356245200/ ('again' the largest firm) (read 2026-10-03)

title: Exxon pulls the plug on its Colorado shale oil project
what: On 2 May Exxon announced it was ending the Colony shale oil project in Colorado, in which it had bought a 60 percent stake only in 1980. The world has too much oil: demand fell in 1981 and OPEC cut its price in October for the first time in its history.
why: The first big retreat: the oil-boom bets of 1979-80 start to unwind as the oil price falls. Exxon's shares drifted lower through the first half of 1982.
source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_ExxonMobil (read 2026-10-03); https://www.upi.com/Archives/1982/01/01/Focus-82-Global-oil-glut-cuts-prices/3355378709200/ (read 2026-10-03)

title: Exxon has quietly bought back a tenth of its own shares
what: Since mid-1983 Exxon has spent more than 3.5 billion dollars buying back about 10 percent of its own stock, at an average of about 41 dollars a share against a recent price of about 50, and it shows no sign of stopping. At the same time it keeps a large exploration programme. Fortune calculates that buying its own shares has been a cheaper way to get oil reserves than drilling for them.
why: The buyback machine that would shrink Exxon's share count for decades and explains much of its steady rise in the 1980s and 1990s, while other oil companies spent their cash on takeovers.
source: https://fortune.com/2012/11/21/beating-the-market-by-buying-back-stock/ (quotes Fortune, 29 April 1985) (read 2026-10-03)

title: The Exxon Valdez runs aground in Alaska
what: Just after midnight on 24 March the tanker Exxon Valdez struck Bligh Reef in Prince William Sound, Alaska, and spilled about 11 million gallons of crude oil. The oil is spreading along a remote and rich coastline. Clean-up costs and lawsuits will follow; how large they will be is unknown.
why: The defining disaster of Exxon's history and its worst reputational moment. Oddly, the share price barely moved: the market judged, correctly, that even billions in costs were small for Exxon. The legal fight lasted until 2008.
source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exxon_Valdez_oil_spill (read 2026-10-03); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_ExxonMobil (read 2026-10-03)

title: Valdez bill of 880 million, and Exxon still raises the dividend
what: Exxon's third-quarter profit fell 9.4 percent to 1.11 billion dollars. In the second quarter it set aside 880 million dollars for cleaning up the Alaska spill, which cut nine-month profit by about a third to 2.54 billion. Even so, Exxon raised its quarterly dividend by 5 cents to 60 cents a share.
why: Shows why the stock shrugged off Valdez: the clean-up was a one-off charge, and the dividend kept rising. Exxon also moved its headquarters from New York to Irving, Texas, in 1989.
source: https://www.upi.com/Archives/1989/10/23/Exxon-earnings-drop-94-percent/2515625118400/ (read 2026-10-03); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_ExxonMobil (HQ move) (read 2026-10-03)

title: Exxon pleads guilty and settles Valdez claims for 1 billion
what: On 8 and 9 October a federal judge in Alaska accepted Exxon's guilty plea and a 1.025 billion dollar settlement with the United States and the state of Alaska. Exxon pays 25 million in criminal fines, 100 million in restitution and 900 million over ten years into a fund to restore Prince William Sound. Lawsuits by fishermen and other Alaskans are not covered and continue.
why: Closes the government side of Valdez at a price Exxon could easily carry; the private damages case stays open for 17 more years.
source: https://www.upi.com/Archives/1991/10/08/Exxon-pleads-guilty-judge-accepts-1-billion-settlement/7997686894400/ (read 2026-10-03); https://evostc.state.ak.us/oil-spill-facts/settlement/ (read 2026-10-03)

title: Anchorage jury orders Exxon to pay 5 billion for the Valdez spill
what: On 16 September a federal jury in Anchorage ordered Exxon to pay 5 billion dollars in punitive damages to about 10,000 fishermen and other Alaskans harmed by the 1989 spill, on top of about 287 million in compensatory damages. It is reported as the largest punitive award ever levied against a corporation.
why: A headline-sized number that the market discounted: the appeals cut it step by step to about 500 million by 2008. Exxon's shares were higher a month later.
source: https://www.deseret.com/1994/9/17/19131402/exxon-ordered-to-pay-5-billion-in-damages/ (read 2026-10-03); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exxon_Valdez_oil_spill (read 2026-10-03)

title: Exxon's profit rises 27 percent
what: Exxon's accounts for 1995 show net income of 6.47 billion dollars, up from 5.10 billion in 1994, and a dividend of 1.50 dollars a share (in today's terms after later splits), up from 1.455. Chemicals earned twice as much as in 1994.
why: The quiet 1990s: rising profits and dividends, a steadily climbing share price with no drama.
source: Exxon Form 10-K405 for 1997, selected financial data (1993-1997, post-split basis), https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/34088/0000930661-98-000526.txt (read 2026-10-03)

title: Exxon splits its shares as profits climb
what: Exxon's board approved a two-for-one stock split on 26 February. Exxon earned 7.51 billion dollars in 1996, up from 6.47 billion in 1995 and 5.10 billion in 1994, and raised its dividend again.
why: The quiet 1990s compounding years: no drama, rising profits and buybacks; the share price roughly doubled from 1994 to 1997.
source: Exxon Form 10-K405 for 1997, https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/34088/0000930661-98-000526.txt (split date, selected financial data) (read 2026-10-03); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lee_Raymond (read 2026-10-03)

title: Exxon and Mobil agree to merge
what: On 1 December Exxon agreed to buy Mobil in a share deal valued at about 76 to 79 billion dollars, the biggest US corporate combination ever: each Mobil share becomes 1.32015 Exxon shares, and Exxon's owners will hold about 70 percent. The deal reunites two pieces of Rockefeller's Standard Oil and needs regulators' approval. With crude below 11 dollars a barrel, the companies plan to cut 9,000 jobs and save 2.8 billion dollars a year. Lee Raymond will run the combined company.
why: The defining deal: made at the bottom of the oil market, it created the company that dominated the 2000s. The share price fell slightly on the day and then rose with oil in 1999.
source: https://dieselnet.com/news/1998/12exxon.php (read 2026-10-03); https://www.baltimoresun.com/news/bs-xpm-1998-12-02-1998336042-story.html (read 2026-10-03); Exxon Form 8-K of 1 December 1998, https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/34088/0000950103-98-001038.txt (read 2026-10-03)

title: OPEC's cuts take effect and oil shares soar
what: On 23 March OPEC and other producers agreed to cut output by a combined 2.1 million barrels a day from 1 April. US crude, about 12 dollars at the end of February, closed April at 18.69 dollars. Exxon's shares jumped as investors bet that the oil glut is ending.
why: Exxon's best month of the 1990s (+18%): the oil price had bottomed, and the Mobil deal looked better with every dollar on the barrel.
source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_world_oil_market_chronology (read 2026-10-03); https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/DCOILWTICO (daily WTI) (read 2026-10-03)

title: ExxonMobil is born
what: The Federal Trade Commission approved the merger on 30 November, after Exxon and Mobil agreed to sell 2,431 petrol stations and other assets, and the deal closed the same day. Shareholders had approved the 81.2 billion dollar merger in May. The new Exxon Mobil Corporation, based in Irving, Texas, is the world's largest oil company and keeps the Exxon, Mobil and Esso brands.
why: The company changes name in the game from December 1999. The merger savings and the oil recovery made the deal look brilliant within a year.
source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_ExxonMobil (FTC approval, 2,431 stations) (read 2026-10-03); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_world_oil_market_chronology (shareholder approval, 81.2 billion) (read 2026-10-03); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lee_Raymond (read 2026-10-03)

title: ExxonMobil earned 17.7 billion dollars in 2000
what: ExxonMobil's annual report shows net income of 17.72 billion dollars for 2000, more than double the 7.91 billion of 1999, on sales of 228 billion. The total includes a 1.73 billion dollar gain from the assets regulators made it sell for the Mobil merger.
why: Proof that the merger worked; the shares held up in 2000-2001 while technology stocks crashed, the classic defensive rotation.
source: ExxonMobil Form 10-K for 2000, https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/34088/000093066101000781/0001.txt (selected financial data) (read 2026-10-03)

title: Profit falls to 11.5 billion in 2002
what: ExxonMobil reported on 30 January that its 2002 net income fell to 11.46 billion dollars from 15.32 billion in 2001, on revenue of 205 billion. Fourth-quarter profit, however, rose 53 percent to 4.09 billion.
why: The dip between the 2000 boom and the 2004-08 super-cycle; the shares had fallen with the market in 2002.
source: ExxonMobil press release of 30 January 2003 (Form 8-K), https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/34088/000003408803000008/ (read 2026-10-03)

title: ExxonMobil's profit nearly doubles to 21.5 billion
what: ExxonMobil said on 29 January that it earned 21.51 billion dollars in 2003, up from 11.46 billion in 2002. The total includes one-off gains, among them a 2.23 billion dollar US tax settlement in the fourth quarter; without them, profit was 17.03 billion.
why: The start of the 2000s oil boom, in which ExxonMobil's profits doubled again within two years.
source: ExxonMobil press release of 29 January 2004 (Form 8-K exhibit 99.1), https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/34088/000003408804000018/r012904ex991.htm (read 2026-10-03); ExxonMobil press release of 31 January 2005 (names the 2.23 billion tax settlement in 4Q03), https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/34088/000003408805000026/r013105ex991.htm (read 2026-10-03)

title: Record profit, full reserves and oil above 50 dollars
what: ExxonMobil reported on 31 January a 2004 profit of 25.33 billion dollars and the highest quarterly profit in its history, 8.42 billion. On 18 February it said it had replaced 112 percent of the oil and gas it produced in 2004, the eleventh year in a row above 100 percent. US crude, about 47 dollars at the end of January, was back above 52 dollars in late February.
why: ExxonMobil's best month since the merger (+23%): the oil boom became undeniable and big oil was re-rated. Most of the gain held for the rest of the decade.
source: ExxonMobil press release of 31 January 2005, https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/34088/000003408805000026/r013105ex991.htm (read 2026-10-03); ExxonMobil press release of 18 February 2005, https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/34088/000003408805000045/r021805ex99.htm (read 2026-10-03); https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/DCOILWTICO (read 2026-10-03)

title: A record 36 billion dollars, and a new boss
what: ExxonMobil reported on 30 January a 2005 profit of 36.13 billion dollars, by far the largest in its history (2004: 25.33 billion), including 10.71 billion in the fourth quarter alone. US crude rose to nearly 70 dollars a barrel last year. Rex Tillerson took over as chief executive on 1 January from Lee Raymond, who retired.
why: Peak of ExxonMobil's public profile: record profits, followed in April 2006 by reports of Raymond's 400 million dollar retirement package. The shares rose 12% this month.
source: ExxonMobil 4Q05 investor relations data summary (Form 8-K of 30 January 2006, exhibit 99.2), https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/34088/000003408806000025/r4q05ex992.htm (read 2026-10-03); ExxonMobil press release of 31 January 2005 (2004 profit), https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/34088/000003408805000026/r013105ex991.htm (read 2026-10-03); https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/DCOILWTICO (read 2026-10-03); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rex_Tillerson (read 2026-10-03); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lee_Raymond (read 2026-10-03)

title: 39.5 billion dollars, another record
what: ExxonMobil reported on 1 February record 2006 net income of 39.5 billion dollars, up from 36.13 billion in 2005, although fourth-quarter profit slipped 4 percent to 10.25 billion as oil prices eased late in the year.
why: The plateau of the super-cycle; the share price rose about a third in 2006 and kept climbing in 2007.
source: ExxonMobil press release of 1 February 2007, https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/34088/000003408807000021/r8k4q07991.htm (read 2026-10-03); https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/MCOILWTICO (read 2026-10-03)

title: Oil hits 145 dollars, then turns
what: US crude closed at a record of about 145 dollars a barrel in early July, then fell back to about 124 by month's end. On 31 July ExxonMobil reported second-quarter profit of 11.68 billion dollars, up 14 percent on a year earlier, but the shares fell as investors worried the oil spike would not last.
why: The top of the commodity super-cycle. ExxonMobil's shares had already peaked in 2007; they fell much less than the market in the crash that followed (-15% in 2008 against about -38% for the S&P 500).
source: https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/DCOILWTICO (read 2026-10-03); ExxonMobil press release of 31 July 2008, https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/34088/000003408808000102/r8k2q991.htm (read 2026-10-03); data/out/xom.json and data/reference/sp500.json (2008 changes, for the why)

title: ExxonMobil buys XTO for 41 billion dollars and bets on shale gas
what: On 14 December ExxonMobil agreed to buy XTO Energy, a leading US producer of natural gas from shale and other 'unconventional' rock, in an all-stock deal valued at 41 billion dollars including 10 billion of XTO debt. XTO shareholders get 0.7098 ExxonMobil shares each, a 25 percent premium.
why: ExxonMobil's big bet on US shale gas, made just before gas prices fell for years; in November 2020 it wrote down US dry gas fields by 17 to 20 billion dollars. Its shares fell 9% this month.
source: ExxonMobil and XTO press release of 14 December 2009, https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/34088/000095010309003246/dp15865_ex9901.htm (read 2026-10-03)

title: Tillerson and Putin's oil chief sign an Arctic deal
what: In August, with Vladimir Putin attending in Sochi, Rex Tillerson and Rosneft's Igor Sechin signed an agreement for ExxonMobil and Russia's state oil company to drill the East-Prinovozemelsky field in the Arctic Ocean, a partnership talked of as worth up to 300 billion dollars.
why: ExxonMobil's Russia bet; its Russian exposure ended with a 3.4 billion dollar charge on the Sakhalin-1 project after the 2022 invasion. Putin awarded Tillerson Russia's Order of Friendship in 2013, four years before he became Secretary of State.
source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rex_Tillerson (read 2026-10-03); ExxonMobil press release of 29 April 2022 (Sakhalin-1 charge), https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/34088/000003408822000023/ (read 2026-10-03)

title: ExxonMobil earned 44.9 billion dollars in 2012
what: ExxonMobil reported on 1 February that it earned 44.88 billion dollars in 2012, up 9 percent from 41.06 billion in 2011 and close to its 2008 record. It spent 39.8 billion dollars on capital projects and exploration.
why: The high plateau before the 2014 bust: huge profits, huge spending, and a share price that rose only modestly between 2011 and 2014.
source: ExxonMobil press release of 1 February 2013, https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/34088/000003408813000003/f8k4q991.htm (read 2026-10-03); ExxonMobil press release of 30 January 2009 (2008 record), https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/34088/000003408809000016/r8k4q991.htm (read 2026-10-03)

title: Oil slides below 70 dollars
what: US crude, about 107 dollars a barrel in late June, closed November at about 66 dollars as a glut builds: US oil production has nearly doubled since 2008 thanks to shale fracking, and Saudi Arabia argues for lower prices to squeeze high-cost shale producers rather than for OPEC cuts. For ExxonMobil, which earned more than 32 billion dollars a year in 2013, every dollar off the oil price cuts profit.
why: The start of ExxonMobil's worst stretch in the game: -68% from April 2014 to October 2020, which ended with it being dropped from the Dow.
source: https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/DCOILWTICO (read 2026-10-03); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010s_oil_glut (read 2026-10-03); ExxonMobil press release of 2 February 2015 (2013 and 2014 earnings), https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/34088/000003408815000004/f8k4q991.htm (read 2026-10-03)

title: ExxonMobil's profit halves
what: ExxonMobil reported on 2 February that it earned 16.15 billion dollars in 2015, half the 32.52 billion of 2014, and 2.78 billion in the fourth quarter, down 58 percent. It cut capital spending by 19 percent. US crude fell to about 26 dollars in mid-February, the lowest in more than a decade.
why: The bottom of the 2014-16 oil bust; ExxonMobil kept paying its dividend, and the shares recovered in 2016.
source: ExxonMobil press release of 2 February 2016, https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/34088/000003408816000053/f8k4q991.htm (read 2026-10-03); https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/DCOILWTICO (read 2026-10-03)

title: Woods's first year: a tax windfall hides a flat quarter
what: ExxonMobil reported on 2 February that it earned 19.71 billion dollars in 2017, the first year under Darren Woods, who took over on 1 January 2017 when Rex Tillerson left to become Secretary of State. But 5.9 billion of the total came from the new US tax law; without it and impairments, fourth-quarter profit was 3.73 billion, slightly lower than a year earlier. The company reported a sixth oil discovery off Guyana.
why: ExxonMobil fell 13% this month, a step in the long 2014-2020 decline; Guyana, barely noticed here, became its best growth asset in the 2020s.
source: ExxonMobil press release of 2 February 2018, https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/34088/000003408818000006/f8k4q991.htm (read 2026-10-03); ExxonMobil Form 8-K of 16 December 2016 (Woods from 1 January 2017), https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/34088/000003408816000103/0000034088-16-000103.txt (read 2026-10-03); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rex_Tillerson (read 2026-10-03)

title: The virus scare hits oil
what: From 20 February stock markets fell sharply as the coronavirus spread beyond China to South Korea, Italy and Iran; in the last week of February Wall Street fell more than 10 percent. Oil fell with them: US crude closed February at about 45 dollars, from 61 at the end of December. ExxonMobil had already reported in January that its 2019 profit fell 31 percent to 14.3 billion dollars.
why: The first leg of the 2020 crash; ExxonMobil fell 17% this month, to its lowest since 2004, before the real collapse in March.
source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_stock_market_crash (read 2026-10-03); https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/DCOILWTICO (read 2026-10-03); ExxonMobil press release of 31 January 2020, https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/34088/000003408820000011/f8k4q991.htm (read 2026-10-03)

title: Price war and pandemic: oil halves in a month
what: On 6 March Russia refused OPEC's proposal to cut output; on 8 March Saudi Arabia announced discounts of 6 to 8 dollars a barrel and more production, and Brent crude fell 30 percent, the biggest drop since the Gulf War. With countries shutting down against the pandemic, US crude closed March at about 20 dollars, from 45 at the end of February.
why: ExxonMobil's worst month in the game (-26%): demand and price collapsed at once, and investors began to doubt its dividend.
source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Russia%E2%80%93Saudi_Arabia_oil_price_war (read 2026-10-03); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_stock_market_crash (read 2026-10-03); https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/DCOILWTICO (read 2026-10-03)

title: ExxonMobil cuts spending by 30 percent as oil goes negative
what: On 7 April ExxonMobil cut its 2020 capital spending by 30 percent, from 33 to about 23 billion dollars, and cash operating costs by 15 percent, mostly in the Permian Basin. On 9 April Saudi Arabia and Russia agreed to cut output by about 10 million barrels a day. On 20 April the US crude price fell below zero, to minus 37 dollars, as storage ran out. Stocks rebounded strongly from their March lows.
why: The rebound month (+22%): the market bet that the worst was priced in and that ExxonMobil could protect its dividend by cutting spending.
source: ExxonMobil press release of 7 April 2020, https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/34088/000003408820000028/f8k1q991.htm (read 2026-10-03); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Russia%E2%80%93Saudi_Arabia_oil_price_war (read 2026-10-03)

title: A vaccine lifts oil shares; ExxonMobil writes off up to 20 billion
what: On 9 November Pfizer and BioNTech said their Covid vaccine was more than 90 percent effective in its first analysis, and oil shares, among the hardest hit by the pandemic, jumped. US crude rose from about 36 to 45 dollars during the month. On 30 November ExxonMobil said it would take a 17 to 20 billion dollar write-down on gas fields it no longer plans to develop, cut spending further and reduce its workforce by 15 percent by the end of 2021, while keeping the dividend.
why: The turn: ExxonMobil's shares had bottomed in October; the vaccine rally (+17% this month) began the climb that made 2021-22 its best two years in the game.
source: Pfizer and BioNTech press release of 9 November 2020 (BioNTech Form 6-K exhibit 99.1), https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1776985/000156459020052228/ (read 2026-10-03); ExxonMobil press release of 30 November 2020, https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/34088/000003408820000093/xomexhibit9911302020.htm (read 2026-10-03); https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/DCOILWTICO (read 2026-10-03)

title: A 20 billion dollar loss, and the shares jump anyway
what: ExxonMobil reported on 2 February a fourth-quarter loss of 20.1 billion dollars, almost all of it write-downs; for 2020 as a whole it lost 22.4 billion dollars. But oil kept rising: US crude passed 60 dollars and closed February at about 62, up from 52 at the end of January. The company says it has cut costs faster than planned.
why: +21% this month: the market looked through the write-offs to the oil recovery. An activist fund, Engine No. 1, was meanwhile campaigning for board seats.
source: ExxonMobil press release of 2 February 2021, https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/34088/000003408821000004/f8k4q991.htm (read 2026-10-03); https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/DCOILWTICO (read 2026-10-03); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ExxonMobil (2020 loss of 22.4 billion) (read 2026-10-03)

title: Oil near 90 dollars and investors rush back to energy
what: US crude rose from about 75 dollars at the end of December to 89 at the end of January, and the monthly average was the highest since 2014. While the S&P 500 fell about 5 percent in January, energy shares were the place to be.
why: ExxonMobil +24% in a month when the S&P 500 fell 5%: the start of the 2022 energy boom.
source: https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/DCOILWTICO (read 2026-10-03); https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/MCOILWTICO (read 2026-10-03); data/reference/sp500.json via data/news/arcs/movers.md (S&P 500 month)

title: ExxonMobil earns almost 20 billion dollars in a quarter
what: ExxonMobil reported on 28 October third-quarter earnings of 19.7 billion dollars, after 17.6 billion in the second quarter, and cash flow of 24.4 billion. Its refineries ran at the highest rates since 2008 and Permian production hit a record. US crude rose from about 80 to 87 dollars during the month. In June President Biden had complained that 'Exxon made more money than God this year'.
why: +27% this month, ExxonMobil's best month in the game: the peak of the 2022 profit boom, in a year when the broad market fell.
source: ExxonMobil press release of 28 October 2022, https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/34088/000003408822000057/f8k3q22991.htm (read 2026-10-03); https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/DCOILWTICO (read 2026-10-03); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ExxonMobil (Biden quote; Q2 2022 earnings) (read 2026-10-03)

title: ExxonMobil buys Pioneer for 59.5 billion dollars
what: On 11 October ExxonMobil agreed to buy Pioneer Natural Resources, a large shale oil producer in the Permian Basin, in an all-stock deal valued at 59.5 billion dollars, or 253 dollars a Pioneer share, an 18 percent premium. Pioneer owners get 2.3234 ExxonMobil shares each. It is ExxonMobil's biggest deal since Mobil and needs regulators' approval.
why: Uses the 2022 windfall and a high share price to double down on US shale; the deal closed in May 2024 and more than doubled ExxonMobil's Permian output.
source: ExxonMobil and Pioneer press release of 11 October 2023 (Form 8-K), https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/34088/000095010323014885/ (read 2026-10-03); ExxonMobil press release of 3 May 2024 (closing), https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/34088/000095010324006322/dp210867_ex9901.htm (read 2026-10-03)

title: Pioneer deal closes; ExxonMobil doubles in the Permian
what: On 3 May ExxonMobil completed its purchase of Pioneer Natural Resources. Its production in the Permian Basin more than doubles to 1.3 million barrels of oil equivalent a day, and it expects about 2 million by 2027, from more than 1.4 million net acres holding an estimated 16 billion barrels.
why: Completes the shale bet; with Guyana it gives ExxonMobil the growth that carried output to a 40-year high in 2025.
source: ExxonMobil press release of 3 May 2024, https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/34088/000095010324006322/dp210867_ex9901.htm (read 2026-10-03)

title: Venezuela, dearer oil and record output lift ExxonMobil
what: After US forces captured Venezuela's president Maduro on 3 January, President Trump met oil executives on 9 January and said they would invest 100 billion dollars there; ExxonMobil's Darren Woods called Venezuela 'uninvestable' under current law, and Trump said he was inclined to keep ExxonMobil out. Oil rose anyway: US crude went from about 57 to 65 dollars during the month as unrest in Iran threatened supply. On 30 January ExxonMobil reported 2025 earnings of 28.8 billion dollars, its highest oil and gas output in more than 40 years and 37.2 billion returned to shareholders.
why: +18% this month, the start of the 2026 surge that the Iran war would turn into an all-time high. The Venezuela spat did not hurt: the market cared about the oil price.

title: War with Iran closes Hormuz and oil passes 100 dollars
what: US and Israeli strikes on Iran began on 28 February. Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, the route for much of the world's oil, and on 9 March Brent crude touched 119.50 dollars, up 29 percent in a day, before settling around 100. US crude averaged about 91 dollars in March, against 65 in February. ExxonMobil, with big production in the Americas, gains from the higher price, though some of its Middle East output is disrupted.
why: ExxonMobil's share price reached its all-time high this month (+11%). The war is the theme writer's beat; this is how it looked from the biggest Western oil company.
